newsitem.title: FRANCE: Race to euro hurts, long-term reform needed - OECD.
newsitem.headline: Race to euro hurts, long-term reform needed - OECD.

text.p: European Union countries racing to cut public deficits for monetary union should set clear targets for longer term reform so that interest rate cuts can be used to protect economic recovery, the OECD said on Thursday.

The Organisation for Economic Co-Operation and Development said in its twice-yearly economic outlook report that the rush to qualify next year for monetary union in 1999 was taking its toll on demand and a fledgling economic recovery.

Clear programmes for genuine medium-term structural reforms could pave the way for cuts in official interest rates to help offset any short-term economic damage without compromising the monetary policy goal of price stability, the report says.

"A forward-looking monetary policy framework, irrespective of the details of monetary policy management, can allow a cut in policy-controlled interest rates to mitigate the short-term negative demand effects of fiscal consolidation," OECD chief economist Kumiharu Shigehara told a news conference.
"Since this policy stance would be geared to offsetting demand weakness, it should not compromise the primary monetary policy goal of achieving and maintaining price stability," he said.
"Nor would monetary policy easing in such a setting be likely to have adverse consequences for long-term interest rates, increases in which would be detrimental to growth."

Several EU countries have recently drawn up spending-cutting 1997 budgets and other austerity measures to get their public deficits down to three percent of gross domestic product next year and qualify to join a single euro currency in 1999.
Japan too is cutting back on public works spending next year and increasing taxes.
"In Europe, fiscal retrenchment is already operating as a negative force on activity," the report says.
"In Japan and much of the European Union...the pace of fiscal consolidation in the near term must also reflect the need to nurture nascent economic recovery."

Shigehara and his colleagues at the Paris OECD headquarters said they were confident that crucial countries such as Germany, France, Italy and Spain could make the EMU qualification test as long as they implemented all the measures promised, and a bit more in some cases.

"I think from our point of view there is too much attention on 1997," another OECD economist, Stephen Potter, said. "Whether that will kill economic recovery is a matter of judgement...we would like to see action on more structural issues."
The EU countries should now be aiming for structural reform beyond 1997 and seeking to get their public deficits well below the three percent mark in the following years, the two men said.
"The basic policy message is that those countries need to be fully committed to reducing structural deficits well below three percent beyond 1997 -- I note structural," Shigehara said.
The OECD forecast economic growth of 2.4 percent next year and 2.7 percent in 1998 after growth of 1.6 percent this year.

It predicts Germany's public deficit overshooting the EMU three-percent marker in 1997, coming in, like Spain's, at 3.4 percent, and France too wide of the mark with 3.2 percent and Italy with 3.7 percent, but says planned measures or further fine-tuning should allow them to reach the target.
Shigehara poured cold water on the idea that mark strength or dollar weakness were the big obstacles to growth, saying consumption rather than exports was the key to recovery.
"It's no longer possible to just rely on exports for growth. I expect business investment to continue to grow. The major issue is how consumption will develop," he said.
"Monetary policy can help short term but you need structural reform," Shigehara told Reuters Financial Television, "It's not just efficiency of the product market but also of the labour market."
